prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at the magic wavelength brought time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: the optical lattice clock, Katori and Ye, as a single prize part. The chair asks whether this is distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and I answer as an experimentalist. The comb gave us the means to count optical cycles. Ion control gave us a single quantum absorber with exquisite isolation but a signal-to-noise limit set by one particle. The lattice clock is a different physical idea: a trap wavelength chosen so that the light shift cancels between the clock levels, which lets thousands of neutral atoms be interrogated at once, Doppler- and recoil-free. That is what moved instability and systematic uncertainty to 1e-18 on practical timescales, and it is the reason the resulting systems have become instruments that see new things: gravitational redshift across a millimetre, many-body interaction shifts in a spin-polarised Fermi gas, tighter bounds on drifts of constants, and sensitivity to dark-matter couplings. Those are results about nature and not only about a better clock. On timing, I see no reason to wait for the redefinition of the second. The performance has been reproduced and surpassed independently at several laboratories and compared across fibre links; the redefinition is a metrological process with its own calendar, and a Nobel recognition of the physics does not depend on it. Having read the whole first round, five of us have converged on the same two names and the same weaknesses, and I take that convergence as a check on my own view and not a substitute for it.
statement.case_against: The attribution gap is real and cannot be closed within a two-name credit. Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Takamoto, Ludlow and Bloom at NIST, and the PTB team each made decisive contributions to the accuracy and stability that the field now takes for granted, and Ye's best results depend on comb and cavity-stabilisation technology recognised in 2005. A sceptic can still call the clock an outstanding refinement of precision spectroscopy and an invention rather than a discovery, as Danielsson and Eriksson note. I accept that this is the committee's weakest point for B056, and I would rather state it openly than argue it away. My answer is that Nobel physics has repeatedly honoured methods that opened new observation, and that the clock has now delivered physics as well as capability, but I recognise that reasonable colleagues weigh that differently. The citation should name the lattice-clock scheme explicitly, so that it does not read as recognising timekeeping twice or as a verdict on parallel groups.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth, as a fellow atomic physicist, ranks B056 first on the strength of the magic-wavelength idea, independent reproduction and its use for redshift, constants and dark-matter searches, and also lists the overlap with 2005 and 2012 as the main reservation.
responses.response: We agree on the substance, and the chair has put the distinctness question to the two of us, so I will state where I land. The distinguishing physics is many-atom interrogation in a trap whose perturbation cancels by design; that removes the single-particle signal-to-noise limit of ion clocks and is not a continuation of the comb. I would also stress to you that the 1e-18 numbers rest on blackbody-radiation control, cryogenic or carefully characterised environments and cavity stability, all of which were developed in several laboratories. That reinforces the case for wording the citation around the lattice scheme itself and for admitting openly that the contributors are more numerous than two. I do not think this changes the names, because Katori's concept and Ye's path to the accuracy and stability frontier are the two clearest links in the chain.

responses.point: Ulf Danielsson moved from the Event Horizon Telescope to B056 after the openings, but says the clock is an invention and measurement capability and that the committee's emphasis is on discovery, so he is unsure it fits.
responses.response: I understand the discomfort and I do not want to answer with rhetoric. I would put it this way: a measurement that moves precision by two orders of magnitude has historically changed what can be asked of nature, and the lattice clock has already done so, with a differential redshift measured over millimetres and with limits on couplings that were out of reach before. I would not claim it has produced a surprise, and I think we should not pretend it has. The claim is that it opened a regime and that the physics has followed. On the many-body side, the observation of interaction effects in a clock that is also a quantum many-body system is a result about matter and not about engineering. If the committee judges that insufficient, that is a legitimate position, but then the same standard should be applied to every instrument-based candidate on our list, including B032 and B034.

responses.point: Bernhard Mehlig supports topological insulators first and the clock second, valuing a simple, general mechanism that was predicted and then confirmed, and he flags his own theory bias.
responses.response: I take your point that B007 is a real discovery with a clean mechanism, and the first-round exchange has moved me to list it as my first alternative, ahead of B032. My difficulty is the same one you name: a Kane, Mele and Molenkamp citation leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp's experiment followed, and the 3D and ARPES work is only partly covered. I cannot yet see a citation wording that makes that gap defensible to a physicist outside the committee. The clock has a compact chain and a record that is independently confirmed, and I do not find the 2016 topology prize alone a decisive objection to B007, but the attribution problem is. I would be prepared to see B007 considered on its merits in a later year or with a different configuration.

responses.point: Eva Olsson prefers spherical-aberration correction (B032) for its documented credit chain and independent reproduction, and asks whether the clock is stronger than she allowed.
responses.response: I think the answer to your question is yes, though for reasons that go beyond counting. Both B032 and B056 are method prizes, and in both cases the question is whether the method opens new observation. For the corrector, what has been opened is mostly atomic-resolution imaging for materials and chemistry, and the physical limit it overcame is the Scherzer limit, which is an instrument limit. For the clock the observables are gravitational and fundamental-constant physics. I also note your own flag about recusal on B032, and I agree it would be prudent to discuss that before the vote. I will keep B032 out of my alternatives for now, because the Krivanek and Nion line is a parallel record I cannot resolve from what we have.

responses.point: Mark Pearce, as chair, places IceCube first and the clock fifth in the opening, then moves the clock to first in round 1, and says he relies on the atomic physicists for B056 detail.
responses.response: Since you rely on us for detail, let me say plainly what the record supports. Reproduction is not a matter of one article: independent laboratories have reported lattice clocks at or beyond the 1e-18 level, and comparisons between them across fibre links are routine. The clock also does not depend on a still-developing source association, which was my concern for IceCube. I fully accept that IceCube is a discovery of a new window, and I would leave it open for a later year when the source identification is more settled. For this year I think the clock is the better-supported of the two, with the caveat that its attribution can only be partly satisfied.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts Katori and Ye as sufficient credit given the parallel work at SYRTE, PTB and NIST, which cannot be accommodated in three names.
Whether a majority reads the lattice clock as a discovery of physics or as an invention of measurement capability; I think the former can be defended but I cannot prove it to a sceptic.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the second, which I judge unnecessary.
Whether B007 could be given a defensible citation that does not exclude Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori, Ye or their laboratories. I disclose again that I am a Lund atomic physicist in the broad AMO community and that I know the quantum-memory field (B023, not shortlisted) closely. WACQT leadership overlaps institutionally with Johansson's Chalmers, which bears on B058 and not on B056. I have no link to the credited names in my alternatives B007 and B034.
